profile.summary: Numbers narrates the journey of Israel in the wilderness, from Sinai to the plains of Moab, while the generation that came out of Egypt is tested by God, and largely falls because of unbelief and rebellion. The book combines historical accounts, laws, lists and speeches to show how the Lord sustains his people, judges disobedience and preserves his promise by raising a new generation to enter the promised land. For evangelical readers, Numbers functions as a great warning and at the same time as a witness of God's persistent fidelity to human infidelity.
profile.setting: After the departure of Egypt, Israel remained about a year in Sinai, where he received the law, and then crossed the desert to the east of the Jordan, encamping in the pitches of Moab before the entrance to Canaan. The geographical and historical scene of the book is linked to pilgrimage in the desert, to the regions of Transjordan and to the end of one generation and beginning of another. The authorship is traditionally attributed to Moses, and the source states that this is the classical Jewish and Christian position; yet, it recognizes that some scholars defend subsequent composition and editing hypotheses. As for the exact date and location of several places, there are uncertainties, and the material itself allows both an older chronology and a later for the exodus and conquest.

structure.label: Organization in the Sinai
structure.description: Initial records of Israel, distribution of the people and the Levites, and preparation for the departure of Mount Sinai.

structure.label: Holiness, order and departure
structure.description: Instructions for community and priestly life, followed by final preparations to leave Sinai.

structure.label: Rebellions and incredulity
structure.description: First episodes of murmuring and refusal to trust the Lord, marking the failure of the generation of the exodus.

structure.label: Judgment in the desert and the history of Balaam
structure.description: New transgressions, divine judgment, preservation of the chosen leadership and then the oracles and episodes linked to Balaam.

structure.label: Purification of the new generation and review of the walk
structure.description: The community is again confronted with infidelity, there is military preparation and then a revision of the desert pilgrimage to Moab.

structure.label: Final provisions for Canaan
structure.description: Guidelines on land, inheritances and final arrangements before entry into Canaan.

themes: Faithfulness of God in the face of human infidelity
Judgment and mercy in the covenant
Formation of a new generation to obey the Lord
Community Holiness, Leadership and Order in God's People
readingKeys: Notice how lists and censuses are not just given, but part of the argument: the first generation falls and another one replaces it.
Read the reports of rebellion as spiritual warnings, linking them to the pattern of unbelief, murmuring, and testing God.
Realize the alternation between judgment and provision: the book insists that the Lord disciplines, but also preserves and leads his people.
profile.cautions: The book contains severe judgments and episodes of rebellion that should be read as theological warning, not as a simple account of unlucky in the desert. Tradition attributes the work to Moses, but the source admits that there is academic debate about composition and editing; therefore, it is appropriate to speak with caution about authorship and date. It is also important not to reduce Numbers to a collection of lists or to a narrative of failure: its center is to show the holy character of God, its patience and the need for obedient faith.

dossier.narratedEra: The book settles in the period of the crossing of Israel through the desert, from the camp at Sinai to the camps of Moab, when the generation that came out of Egypt is being replaced by another before the entrance to Canaan. The notes describe three internal moments: the preparation for from Sinai, the long journey of forty years and the final months on the banks of the Jordan (Nm 1:1-10:10; 10:11'22:1; 21:1'36:13).
dossier.compositionEra: The tradition presented in the notes attributes the book to Moses as the main author, possibly with supervision of compilation and even dictated parts of the text. At the same time, it is admitted that later scribes and editors may have made additions or adjustments. The modern documentary hypothesis is mentioned as speculative, and the final form of the book is treated as substantially mosaic, without excluding later editorial interventions.

politics.title: Mosaic leadership in the national organization
politics.detail: Moses leads the census, receives the divine will and organizes the march of the community. A tribe leader is assigned to assist in the census, showing a tribal political structure under prophetic mediation.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of Numbers is not only devotional; it shows how the nation is born under central command, but articulated by recognizable tribal leaders.

politics.title: Priestly hierarchy and limits of authority
politics.detail: Aaron, his sons and the Levites receive distinct roles. Priests have exclusive access to the central functions of the sanctuary, while the Levites serve as assistants and guardians, with death penalty for unauthorized access.
politics.readingImpact: The political-religious conflict in Israel is read as a matter of legitimate borders: who can represent the people before the Lord and who cannot.

politics.title: Crisis of authority and need for clear borders
politics.detail: The instructions of Numbers 18 are presented in response to the need evidenced in Numbers 17 to clearly define the limits between people, priests and Levites.
politics.readingImpact: Israel's community order appears as a reaction to internal disputes; holiness regulates the camp policy.

politics.title: Disputes for tribal inheritance and territorial stability
politics.detail: The decision in favour of Zelofeade's daughters creates standards to prevent the loss of land between tribes by marriage. The rules preserve the continuity of the tribal portions, including in the tribe of José/Manassés.
politics.readingImpact: The book shows land policy rather than monarchy: Israel's integrity is protected by the maintenance of tribal portions.

politics.title: Arrangements for the occupation of Transjordan and Canaan
politics.detail: The notes summarize that there were arrangements for the settlement in Transjordan, followed by expectation of the occupation of Canaan and the entry of the new generation.
politics.readingImpact: The number policy is the policy of the distribution of land and military preparation, not that of kings or empires appointed in the notes.

customs.title: Tribal and family structure of society
customs.detail: The Hebrew culture is described as tribal, organized into clans and families; tribal leaders are identifiable and act as recognized representatives.
customs.readingImpact: The genealogical and tribal lists are not bureaucratic details: they show how Israel's collective identity was preserved.

customs.title: Men apt for war from twenty years
customs.detail: The census brings together men aged twenty or more, able to go to war, and measures the nation's fighting force.
customs.readingImpact: Military preparation is part of the daily life of the people in the desert; the crossing is read as a march of conquest, not just religious pilgrimage.

customs.title: Levitical service as sacred work
customs.detail: The Levites do not enter the military count because their role is to disassemble, transport, protect and, at certain times, assemble the tabernacle. His work is described as a specialized and separate service.
customs.readingImpact: Numbers portray a division of labor in which the cult organizes community life and defines concrete social functions.

customs.title: Sustained through offers and tithes
customs.detail: Priests and Levites are kept by the sacrificial system and tithes. The text explains that this works as compensation/wage for the service to the tabernacle, including part of the offerings and tithe tithe.
customs.readingImpact: The cultual economy of Numbers shows that cult, food and material support were integrated.

customs.title: Redemption of the firstborn and payment in silver
customs.detail: The firstborn and certain unclean animals need to be rescued for a rate in silver, because they cannot be sacrificed. This puts domestic life under the logic of consecration to the Lord.
customs.readingImpact: Israel's families live under economic and ritual rules that link birth, property, and worship.

customs.title: Marriage and inheritance inside the paternal house
customs.detail: Zelofeade's daughters marry cousins on the paternal side to conserve the father's inheritance within the clan. The note states that this marriage between cousins was acceptable in ancient Hebrew society.
customs.readingImpact: Family life is read in the light of land preservation; marriage is not only a private matter, but a mechanism of tribal continuity.

language.title: Title "Numbers" and Hebrew "
language.detail: The Portuguese title derives from the Latin Numeri and the Greek Arithmoi, linked to the counts of the book. In the Hebrew Bible, the book is called "the desert," the word taken of Nm 1:1.
language.readingImpact: The Hebrew title emphasizes the setting; the traditional title in Portuguese highlights the census structure. The two keys guide the reading.

language.title: Structure by travel and two census
language.detail: The notes organize the book in three stages of the pilgrimage and in two censuses, one in Sinai and the other in the campinas of Moab. The contrast between the two generations is a central structural resource.
language.readingImpact: The literary form reinforces the theme of the replacement of the rebel generation by a new generation able to enter the land.

language.title: Mixture of narrative, poetry, law and lists
language.detail: Numbers contain narrative, poetry, law, lists of numbers, offers and itineraries. The note also mentions that the NLT organizes certain lists in concise name and number tables.
language.readingImpact: The reader needs to alternate between genres; the book is not read as a simple continuous narrative, but as a varied composition of records.

language.title: Old literary sources cited by the text itself
language.detail: The notes mention sources such as the Book of the Lord's Wars, the "Canticle of the Well" and the "Cântico of Hesbom"; they also suggest that Nm 31:32-47 can be based on a real record of spoils and Nm 33 in a written diary.
language.readingImpact: This suggests that the book preserves memory and old documents, rather than inventing the whole tradition abstractly.

language.title: Poetic difficult texts and textual preservation
language.detail: The poetry of Numbers 21-24 is described as difficult to interpret, but the Hebrew text is considered very well preserved compared to the Dead Sea Scrolls. The differences between the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch are treated as deliberate differences of interpretation.
language.readingImpact: The reading must respect the hardness of the poetic passages without forcing harmonizations; at the same time, the textual transmission is seen as stable.

timeline.title: Year following the exodus: beginning of the organization in Sinai
timeline.detail: The notes place Nm 1:1 in the year after the departure of Israel from Egypt, when God continued to communicate his will through Moses in the tabernacle.
timeline.readingImpact: The book begins with the newly liberated nation, still in institutional formation, before entering the earth.

timeline.title: nineteen days of preparation to get out of Sinai
timeline.detail: The introduction divides the beginning of the book into a stage of nineteen days of preparation to leave Sinai, before the march to the promised land.
timeline.readingImpact: The displacement is not immediate; there is a preparatory period of worship, census and military organization.

timeline.title: Forty years of journey and death of the rebel generation
timeline.detail: The narrative covers a thirty-nine-year journey between Sinai and Moab, inserted in the total period of forty years in the desert. The generation of the exodus dies in the wilderness, except for Joshua and Caleb.
timeline.readingImpact: The long-lasting interpretation of the desert as divine discipline because of unbelief, not as a geographical accident.

timeline.title: Last months in the campinas of Moabe
timeline.detail: The third phase of the book is located in the final months of Israel's camp in Moab, just before the entry into Canaan.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader should read the final chapters as immediate preparation for the possession of the earth and not as distant history.

timeline.title: Absolute date of exodus and conquest remains debated
timeline.detail: The notes state that the geographical, cultural and linguistic data of Numbers adjust to both an early date and a late date for exodus and conquest, proposed in the 1400s or 1200 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: The setting of the book does not solve its absolute historical date alone; the chronology continues to be debated.

timeline.title: Ancient and medieval textual preservation
timeline.detail: The Masoretic Text is dated in the notes of the period of the 900 years AD, while the Qumran manuscripts used for comparison are between 150 BC and 125 AD.
timeline.readingImpact: The history of transmission helps to distinguish between the narrated epoch and the later history of the text.
timeline.reference: Nm 21-24; textual transmission of the book

investigation: Mosaic authorship is the traditional position presented, but the notes also admit compilation and subsequent editing; the documental hypothesis is mentioned as speculative.
The names of many places in the desert itinerary cannot be identified for sure, and the archaeological material of Sinai, Negeb and Transjordan is relevant, but not conclusive.
The numbers of the census were interpreted in different ways: literal, symbolic, projected from later or misunderstood period in translation.
There are difficult poetic excerpts in Nm 21-24; the textual comparison shows general stability, but also interpretive differences between textual traditions.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the attached notes of Tyndale Open Study Notes and Matthew Henry, both with introductory focus and confessional Protestant reading. Coverage is selective: there are good observations on census, Levites, inheritance, genealogy, literary genres, sources and textual transmission, but little detailed information about international politics, foreign economy or everyday life outside the Israeli camp. No gaps were filled with external knowledge; therefore, items about empires, kings, or absolute dates appear only when the notes directly or debated them. Also, no events from other books have been mixed without explicit support from the sources.
